claims.text: Mild service-relevant thermal exposure triggers nucleation and controlled growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases from the metastable solid solution.
The kinetics and spatial distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases determine whether oxidation and corrosion resistance are retained or lost.
A fine, uniform intermetallic distribution promotes a coherent protective oxide at interfacial regions.
Coarsening or excessive intermetallic formation depletes elements needed for matrix passivation and consequently degrades oxidation and corrosion resistance.
The initial alloy is an as-cast, homogeneous, non-equilibrium metastable solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
Aging near the lower boundary of the phase-transformation regime can induce progressive intermetallic formation without causing complete phase transformation.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment is suitable for evaluating corrosion behavior in the proposed controlled comparison.
The newly formed Mg-rich intermetallic phases preferentially occur along grain or phase boundaries.
Thermal decomposition begins through local Mg partitioning and produces nanoscale intermetallic precipitates by nucleation and growth.
Early-stage aged samples will contain a fine, well-distributed population of Mg-rich intermetallics.
Early-stage aged samples will retain or improve oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Excessive aging will produce coarser intermetallics correlated with a measurable decline in oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Below a critical thermal exposure, transformation is minimal and performance remains similar to the baseline.
Above the critical thermal exposure, excessive coarsening causes performance degradation.
